_readme: Worked examples shown under 'Load an example' in the Workload profile and used as reference patterns in the workshop playbook. Each example sets workload inputs (on top of the workload defaults in assumptions.json), optional data changes (same format as share links: assumptions → s: {path: value}), and the verdict it is expected to produce. scripts/check_examples.js re-checks every verdict after the daily price update and flags any that change, so the app, the playbook and the expected results stay in step. Keep descriptions technical and free of dollar figures, which drift as prices update.

examples.name: Pilot: employee copilot, 500 users
examples.summary: Low volume: owned GPUs would sit about 1% busy.
examples.note: A pilot this size cannot keep even one server busy, and owned hardware is paid for around the clock whether it is used or not. Paying per token follows actual usage.
examples.try: Raise [[Users|users]] to 20,000. It still favors the API: office-hours traffic leaves owned GPUs idle overnight and on weekends.

examples.name: Company-wide copilot, approved API providers only
examples.summary: 20,000 users; only providers the customer has approved are compared.
examples.note: Leaving out the lowest-cost routed provider raises the per-token price enough that owning a baseline for the steady daytime load and sending busy-hour overflow to an approved API becomes cheapest.
examples.try: Under Advanced settings → [[API providers to compare|api_excluded]], tick OpenRouter back on. The answer flips to paying per token.

examples.name: 24/7 contact center, 2,000 agents
examples.summary: Steady traffic every day of the month keeps owned GPUs busy.
examples.note: With demand spread across every day and most hours, owned servers stay busy enough to beat paying per token. One right-sized server carries almost every token; the busiest minutes wait a few seconds instead of paying for a bigger setup, so no hybrid is needed.
examples.try: Set [[Active days per month|active_days_per_month]] to 21.7 and [[Busy-hour share|busy_hour_share_pct]] to 15% (office hours only). Utilization drops and paying per token becomes cheaper.

examples.name: Software development assistant, 5,000 developers
examples.summary: Long prompts (6,000 tokens) and fast responses (40 tokens/sec) raise the hardware needed.
examples.note: GPU memory for long contexts, not raw speed, sets how many servers are needed. Owning most of the capacity and sending the overflow to an API is cheapest.
examples.try: Lower [[Avg input tokens|avg_input_tokens]] to 2,000 (smaller context per request). One server now covers the busiest hour with waits of a couple of seconds, so owning wins. Then set [[Acceptable wait|peak_wait_s]] to “No waiting” and watch the answer change.

examples.name: Continuous document processing (schedulable batch)
examples.summary: Queued work spread evenly across 24 hours keeps GPUs about half busy.
examples.note: Work that is not latency-sensitive can be queued and spread across available capacity instead of arriving in an interactive peak. High, steady utilization makes owning cheapest even against discounted batch API pricing.
examples.try: Set [[Busy-hour share|busy_hour_share_pct]] to 15% (an interactive, office-hours peak). Owning for that peak gets expensive and a hybrid mix wins.

examples.name: Small batch workload that will grow
examples.summary: The same queued work at a much smaller volume: paying per token is slightly cheaper today.
examples.note: Even the smallest server would be lightly used at this volume, so paying per token edges it out. Owning catches up at a few times today's volume; the Breakeven tab shows where the lines cross.
examples.try: Raise [[Users|users]] to 400 (about 2.5× today) and watch the result cross over to owning.

examples.name: Dedicated GPUs, no data center
examples.summary: Dedicated GPUs required; owning includes colocation and operations staff.
examples.note: Every API provider is left out because the model must run on dedicated GPUs. Owning adds colocation and half an engineer. Rented GPUs still need about a quarter of an engineer for model serving, drivers and monitoring, but no facility or hardware lifecycle.
examples.try: In Data editor → Assumptions, set [[onprem ops_fte|@assumptions:onprem.ops_fte]] to 0 and untick [[colo_enabled|@assumptions:onprem.colo_enabled]] (the customer already has a data center and a team). Owning becomes cheaper.

onprem.ops_fte.source: Example: half an engineer to run owned servers

cloud.ops_fte.source: Example: a quarter of an engineer to run the model on rented GPUs
